How to Read a Creator Media Kit

Growth

In short: A creator media kit is a sales document prepared by the seller. Read past the follower count to median engagement, real demographics and repeat sponsors, ask for the numbers it leaves out, and test on cost-per-outcome terms before buying a package.

Key points

  • Follower count is the least informative figure and the most prominently displayed.
  • Ask for median engagement over the last thirty posts, not the average over the best ten.
  • Past partner logos show who paid once, not who paid twice, which is the figure that matters.
  • Ask whether the creator will accept cost-per-outcome terms with a tracked link for a first piece.
  • Match the kit's numbers to the job: awareness, explanation, conversion or specialist authority.

A media kit is the document a creator or publisher sends to a company considering paying them: audience size, demographics, engagement, past partners, formats offered, and rates. It is a sales document, prepared by the seller, and it should be read as one.

What is usually in it

Audience size by platform: followers, subscribers, monthly listeners, newsletter recipients.

Engagement metrics: average likes, comments, shares, views, open rates, click rates.

Audience demographics: age, gender, location, sometimes income and interests, drawn from platform analytics.

Past partners: logos of companies that have paid before.

Formats and rates: a dedicated post, a mention, a story, a video integration, a newsletter placement, with prices for each, and sometimes packages.

Case studies: a past campaign with results.

What each number means, and what it hides

Follower count is the least informative figure and the one most prominently displayed. It includes inactive accounts, bots, and people who followed years ago for a different reason. On platforms where reach is algorithmic, followers barely predict how many people see a post.

Average engagement is more useful, and is routinely calculated on the creator's best-performing recent posts. Ask for the median over the last thirty posts, not the average over the best ten.

Demographics come from platform analytics and are reasonably reliable for age, gender, and country. They say nothing about whether the audience buys the category. A finance creator's audience may be mostly other finance creators.

Past partners tell you who paid once. They do not tell you who paid twice, which is the figure that matters.

Rates are a starting position. They vary by month, by how full the creator's calendar is, and by whether the deal is flat or performance-based.

The numbers that are not on it

Audience overlap with other creators the company is considering. Share of audience in the geographies the product serves. Evidence that the audience has adopted products the creator recommended before. Retention: how many people who came through this creator last time are still customers. Whether the creator will accept cost-per-outcome terms, which reveals more about their confidence in their audience than any slide. And the creator's other commercial relationships, including competitors and, in crypto, tokens they hold.

The questions to ask

May we see platform analytics directly, screen-shared, for the last ninety days? What did the last three sponsors in our category see, and may we speak to one? What share of your audience is in our markets? Would you do a first piece on a cost-per-outcome basis, with a tracked link, before we discuss a package? What are your current paid relationships, and are any in our category? What disclosure language do you use, and where does it appear?

A creator who answers those readily is a professional with a real audience. A creator who returns to the follower count has told you what the media kit was for.

Read it against the job

The kit describes the creator. The decision depends on the job: awareness, explanation, conversion, or authority in a specialist audience. A large, lightly engaged audience may suit the first and fail at the rest. A small, deeply trusting audience may do the opposite. Match the kit's numbers to the job, test small before committing, and pay for the outcome the job requires.

lowob takeaway: A media kit is a sales document. Read past the follower count to median engagement, real demographics, and repeat sponsors; ask for the numbers it omits; and test on cost-per-outcome terms before buying a package.

Common questions

How do I evaluate an influencer's media kit?

Treat it as a sales document. Look past follower count to median engagement, platform-sourced demographics and repeat sponsors, and ask for platform analytics directly for the last ninety days.

What questions should I ask a creator before sponsoring them?

Ask to see analytics screen-shared, what the last three sponsors in your category saw, what share of the audience is in your markets, whether they will do a first piece on cost-per-outcome terms, and what paid relationships they have.

Are creator engagement rates reliable?

Average engagement is routinely calculated on the creator's best recent posts. Ask for the median over the last thirty posts instead.

What is missing from most media kits?

Audience overlap with other creators, share of audience in your geographies, evidence of past product adoption, retention of customers they sent, and their other commercial relationships, including token holdings in crypto.
